facts.title: What Medicare is
facts.text: Medicare is health insurance from the federal government. It helps pay for health care. It is mainly for people 65 or older who meet the program’s eligibility rules. Some younger people qualify because of a disability, End-Stage Renal Disease, or ALS. You can learn the coverage pieces one at a time.
facts.summary: Medicare is federal health insurance. We’ll build the rest of the picture one piece at a time.
facts.question: What is Medicare?

facts.title: The two coverage routes
facts.text: Original Medicare is Parts A and B through the federal program. Medicare Advantage is a private plan approved by Medicare that provides Parts A and B. Both routes provide Medicare coverage, with different rules and costs. We can add the other coverage pieces after this distinction is clear.
facts.summary: You can get Parts A and B through the federal program or through a private Medicare Advantage plan.
facts.question: What are the two ways to get Medicare?

facts.title: The piece for prescription medicines
facts.text: Part D helps pay for prescription medicines. Each drug plan has a list of covered medicines and its own costs and rules. A medicine list is a starting point for checking those details; it does not establish personal coverage or pharmacy prices.
facts.summary: Part D is Medicare coverage for prescription medicines. Your medicine list helps identify what to check.
facts.question: What does Part D do?

facts.title: How your options fit together
facts.text: There are two main routes. Original Medicare is Parts A and B; you can add a separate drug plan and may be able to buy Medigap to help with your share of costs. Medicare Advantage provides A and B through a private plan, and most plans include drug coverage. Medigap goes with Original Medicare, not Medicare Advantage. You still pay the Part B premium with either route.
facts.summary: Start with hospital and medical care. Then compare the two ways to get your coverage.
facts.question: How do my Medicare options fit together?

facts.title: The two parts to start with
facts.text:
Part A: Hospital insurance: inpatient hospital care, skilled nursing facility care, hospice and some home health care.

Part B: Medical insurance: doctors, outpatient care, tests, equipment and many preventive services.

Parts A and B together, run by the federal government and accepted by any U.S. doctor who takes Medicare.
facts.summary: Part A is hospital insurance. Part B is medical insurance. Together, they are Original Medicare.
facts.question: What do Parts A and B cover?

facts.title: Part A: hospital care
facts.text: Part A is hospital insurance. It covers inpatient hospital care, skilled nursing facility care, hospice, and some home health care. Together, Part A and Part B are Original Medicare.
facts.summary: Hospital insurance is one part of Medicare.
facts.question: What is Part A?

facts.title: Part B: medical care
facts.text: Part B is medical insurance. It covers doctors, outpatient care, tests, equipment, and many preventive services. Together, Part A and Part B are Original Medicare.
facts.summary: Medical insurance is one part of Medicare.
facts.question: What is Part B?

facts.title: Original Medicare
facts.text: Parts A and B together, run by the federal government and accepted by any U.S. doctor who takes Medicare. You can add separate drug coverage (Part D) and may be able to buy a Medigap policy for certain A/B costs.
facts.summary: Parts A and B are the foundation. Other coverage can help with drugs and some costs.
facts.question: What is Original Medicare?

facts.title: Medicare Advantage
facts.text: Medicare hospital and medical coverage through a private insurance company’s plan instead of Original Medicare. Most plans include drug coverage. Doctors, costs, and rules vary by plan. You still pay the Part B premium. Check each plan's doctors, drug coverage, costs, and rules.
facts.summary: A private plan provides Parts A and B. Most plans also include drug coverage.
facts.question: What is Medicare Advantage?

facts.title: Where prescription coverage fits
facts.text: Part D helps pay for prescription medicines. With Original Medicare, you can join a separate Medicare drug plan. Most Medicare Advantage plans include Part D. Check the exact drug list, restrictions, pharmacy, and costs before relying on coverage for a particular medicine.
facts.summary: Drug coverage is called Part D. Where it sits depends on the coverage route.
facts.question: How do I get prescription drug coverage?

facts.title: What a supplement does
facts.text: Medicare Supplement Insurance, a private policy that helps pay your share of costs under Original Medicare. Same thing as a Supplement. It works with Original Medicare, not Medicare Advantage. Drug coverage is separate. Check your enrollment rights before changing existing coverage.
facts.summary: Medigap can help pay your share of certain Original Medicare costs.
facts.question: What is Medigap?

facts.title: Dental, vision, and hearing
facts.text: Original Medicare generally does not cover routine dental, vision, and hearing services. Some Medicare Advantage plans include benefits, with conditions and limits. Check covered services, costs, yearly limits, and providers for the exact plan.
facts.summary: Routine services need a separate check. Benefits can differ from plan to plan.
facts.question: How do dental, vision, and hearing benefits work?

facts.title: Monthly cost and care costs
facts.text: A premium is the amount you pay each month for coverage. A deductible is an amount you pay before coverage pays its share under the benefit's rules. Copays and coinsurance are costs when you use care. A plan's premium alone is not your total cost.
facts.summary: A monthly premium and what you pay when you use care are different costs.
facts.question: What costs should I compare?

facts.title: What to check for each plan
facts.text: No. Records are in source order or ordered by explicit published fields. Eligibility, doctor participation, exact medicines and personal total cost have not been established. Compare the exact plan's providers, drug coverage, costs, and enrollment requirements before making a decision.
facts.summary: A plan list is the starting point. Check doctors, medicines, and costs for your situation.
facts.question: What should I check before choosing a plan?

facts.title: Dates depend on your situation
facts.text: A birthday and current work coverage do not establish when Part B actually starts. Social Security confirms the enrollment route and effective date. Unknown dates stay unknown. The timeline uses the facts entered in this tab. An unknown date stays an open check; special enrollment rights may need separate confirmation.
facts.summary: Your birth date, actual coverage, and job insurance can affect which dates need checking.
facts.question: Why do these dates matter?

facts.title: Turn your map into next steps
facts.text: Use the checklist to confirm open coverage questions, dates, doctor participation, and medicine costs. It includes official tools and help contacts. Saving a plan for comparison does not enroll you or establish that it fits your needs.
facts.summary: Keep the facts you entered and work through the checks that remain open.
facts.question: How do I use my checklist?

facts.title: Medical spending limits
facts.summary: Premiums, medical cost sharing and drug costs are separate.
facts.question: What does a medical spending limit mean?
facts.text: A Medicare Advantage limit applies to covered medical cost sharing. Premiums and drug costs are separate. Original Medicare Parts A and B have no yearly medical spending cap on their own.
facts.provenance: Retained GLOSSARY.yearly out-of-pocket limit in app.js, meaning unchanged.

facts.title: Check switching rights
facts.summary: Switching rights need checking separately from the policy benefits.
facts.question: Why check Medigap timing before changing coverage?
facts.text: The federal six-month age-65 Medigap period depends on both age and Part B enrollment. Insurers cannot use medical underwriting to refuse a policy or charge more because of health during this period; other conditions and special rights may still matter.
